text.p: PTT Exploration and Production Plc, once the darling of Thai energy stocks, has seen its share price drop almost 20 percent in recent weeks, but most analysts say its solid fundamentals still make it a good long-term buy.
Shares of PTTEP, the exploration arm of state-run Petroleum Authority of Thailand, reached an all-time high of 410 baht on January 23. On Monday they were down eight baht to 310 baht.
The fall has been due to jitters over a sharp reduction of its possible and probable reserves, and a likely credit ratings downgrade by Moody's Investor's service.
But analysts say PTTEP's bull run, which saw it out-perform the market during bearish 1996, may not be over.
While the market seems divided over its short-term prospects, most analysts agreed PTTEP's solid fundamentals would make it a good long-term investment.

"We recommend PTTEP as a long-term buy. The share price will be determined by its net asset. However, near-term, the share price will still be volatile because its projects are mostly long-term," said Gordon Kwan of Daiwa Securities in Hong Kong.
Thailand's steadily rising demand for energy, forecast to grow at least 10 percent in the next five years, and PTTEP's projected increase of natural gas production were cited as supporting factors.
"We expect the natural gas production of the company to triple between 1997-2000," said Robin Shoemaker, Lehman Brothers' Associate Director of Asian Research.
"So, there is a significant increase in production in gas that lies ahead. We believe that will increase the asset value per share of the company," he said.

The company produced 14 million barrels of crude equivalent (MMBOE) in 1996. PTTEP has forecast that its sales would surge to 124,000 barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) per day by the year 2001, from 37,500 BOE per day in 1996.

PTTEP's current projects include its main Bongkot and Pailin fields in the Gulf of Thailand, the controversial Moattama and Yetagun projects in Burma's Gulf of Martaban, and the onshore S-1 and E-5 fields.
The company is also expected to announce the size of natural gas reserves in the Thai-Malaysian Joint Development Area by the second half of this year.
The market also expects the company to move into the big Natuna Gas Project in Indonesian waters, a move that could substantially boost its net assets.
PTTEP president Prajya Phinyawat told Reuters in a recent interview that the company was likely to farm into Natuna if its parent firm, PTT, decides to buy natural gas from the source.
PTTEP's proven reserves as of December 1996 were 502 MMBOE, a three percent increase from 1995. But the probable and possible reserves dropped by 342.7 MMBOE to 527.7.

"I think the market overreacted to the (news of downgrade) because the possible and probable reserves are very volatile. It's the proven reserves category that is the most important," said Lehman's Shoemaker.
He said his firm believes the share price would reach 450 baht within a year and has recommended PTTEP as a buy.
Some analysts, like Asia Equity's Malcolm Lui, said the recent weakness in crude oil prices would mean lower product prices for PTTEP.
Lehman's Shoemaker disagreed.
"The world oil prices were very high during the winter months, but we see it slightly lower in 1997 than in 1996. And that will affect the price of gas from the Gulf of Thailand," he said.
